detail.extracted_title: When Local Value Crosses Borders: Dr. Abeer Al Kalbani on Taking Omani Suppliers Global
detail.excerpt: In-Country Value specialist Dr. Abeer bint Ali Al Kalbani examines why owning foreign equity differs from building domestic capability—and how Oman’s next phase of localization rests on equipping local suppliers to win unshielded international contracts.
detail.article_html:
For years, conversations around In-Country Value in Oman focused on what happens inside national borders: how much domestic procurement stays at home, how many local suppliers enter industrial supply chains, and how quickly national talent replaces imported services. Yet as Omani sovereign funds acquire stakes abroad, national companies operate across multiple jurisdictions, and deepwater ports link Duqm to European industrial corridors, a sharper economic question comes into view: what makes value genuinely “local” once capital and firms cross borders?

In the second part of her analytical series in Oman Daily, In-Country Value specialist Dr. Abeer bint Ali Al Kalbani draws a clear line between owning an overseas asset and expanding the productive power of the home economy. Acquiring a stake in a foreign technology company can deliver strong dividends and preserve sovereign wealth—an entirely valid investment goal measured on financial terms—while leaving research teams, engineering routines, and practical know-how untouched in their original headquarters.

Ownership Versus Absorptive Capacity

Capital and share certificates can cross continents in an afternoon; industrial capability accumulates far more slowly. To explain why, Al Kalbani turns to what economists call absorptive capacity: the domestic institutions, technical specialists, and industrial firms able to grasp external knowledge, adapt it, and put it to work inside Oman’s own production base.

Without that domestic foundation, access to advanced technology on paper rarely alters how local factories or engineering offices actually operate. Conversely, a comparatively modest external partnership that opens a new export market, secures an international certification, or embeds a local Omani firm inside a demanding supply chain can permanently upgrade what the national economy knows how to make and deliver. Evaluating outbound investment accurately therefore starts by distinguishing financial return from productive transfer—crediting sovereign wealth preservation on its own merits without assuming unmeasured industrial spillover at home.

Head-Start Preference and the Ceiling of Protection

That domestic foundation brings localization policy back to center stage from a fresh angle. Directed local procurement gives fledgling Omani suppliers a vital head start, justifying early investments in specialized machinery, technical training, and industry certifications while helping firms weather initial learning costs.

Yet Al Kalbani argues that the true economic worth of domestic preference lies in shrinking the need for protection over time rather than extending it indefinitely. In tradable sectors, international competition offers a revealing maturity test. Foreign buyers care nothing about Oman’s domestic localization targets; their purchasing decisions rest strictly on price, quality, technical accreditation, reliability, and on-time delivery. When an Omani supplier wins business abroad—and keeps winning without its original domestic preference—localization policy proves it has built genuine competitive muscle rather than permanent reliance on sheltered demand.

From Duqm Hydrogen Corridors to Export Readiness

Nowhere is that shift clearer than in Oman’s expanding “economy of connection.” Through green hydrogen and derivatives agreements with the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany, the Sultanate is linking clean production in Duqm to ports, storage terminals, and industrial demand centers across Northwest Europe. Beyond shipping molecules, those corridors open vast demand for engineering design, specialized logistics, maritime transport, terminal storage, inspection, certification, and operational maintenance.

Whether Omani companies capture that surrounding value depends on bridging the gap between diplomatic market access and firm-level readiness. “A market may be legally open, yet firms remain unable to enter it due to gaps in financing, accreditation, or distribution networks—highlighting why supplier support must evolve from local preference to qualifying firms for external competition,” Al Kalbani writes. Trade agreements and economic diplomacy lower entry barriers at the border, while export finance, international accreditation programs, and links to global procurement networks enable Omani suppliers to step through the door.

Additionality and Completing the Capability Cycle

To judge when cross-border expansion truly strengthens the national economy, Al Kalbani proposes applying the test of additionality: tracing what changed directly because of an external partnership or export push compared with what would have happened anyway. Following an anchor client abroad is a promising first step, while winning independent contracts across wider markets—and bringing higher-value engineering, management, and production routines back into Oman—completes the capability cycle. Cross-border growth then reinforces localization rather than diluting it, giving Omani-built expertise a larger arena to scale before returning deeper strength to the economy where it began.

detail.instagram_caption:
Buying equity in an overseas technology firm can generate sovereign financial returns, yet knowledge stays abroad unless institutions and specialists at home possess the absorptive capacity to put it to work. In her latest economic analysis, In-Country Value specialist Dr. Abeer bint Ali Al Kalbani explores what makes value truly local once Omani capital, ports, and suppliers operate across borders.

Directed domestic procurement gives local firms an essential head start to fund equipment, certifications, and early learning curves. Still, the real measure of localization policy is whether it reduces the need for sheltered demand over time—proven when Omani suppliers win unshielded foreign contracts judged strictly on price, quality, technical accreditation, and reliable delivery.

As Oman builds green hydrogen and derivatives corridors linking Duqm with industrial ports in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Germany, vast opportunities are emerging across engineering, specialized logistics, storage, and inspection. Turning open trade channels into real contracts requires shifting ICV tools toward export finance, international accreditation, and global buyer networks—so cross-border growth feeds higher-value capability back into Oman's home economy.

Read the full analysis at omanspire.om (link in bio).
